content: Malnutrition is a prevalent issue among patients awaiting orthotopic liver transplantation and is associated with an increased risk of complications following the procedure. The timing and selection of enteral or parenteral nutrition for these patients remain subjects of ongoing debate. Additionally, the impact of nutritional supplements administered either before or after liver transplantation is not well understood. The purpose of this review was to evaluate the potential benefits and harms of enteral and parenteral nutrition, as well as oral nutritional supplements, in patients undergoing liver transplantation. To achieve this, a comprehensive search was conducted across multiple databases, including the Cochrane Hepato-Biliary Group Controlled Trials Register, MEDLINE, EMBASE, and others, covering studies published up to March 2012. Experts in the field were consulted, and relevant journals and conference proceedings were manually reviewed. The review included randomized clinical trials with either parallel or cross-over designs that assessed the effects of these nutritional interventions. Two independent reviewers evaluated the risk of bias in the studies and extracted data. Dichotomous outcomes were expressed as odds ratios (OR), while continuous outcomes were reported as mean differences (MD), both with 95% confidence intervals (CI). Due to the clinical heterogeneity of the interventions, meta-analysis was not feasible. Thirteen trials met the inclusion criteria, but four of these did not report outcomes that were pre-specified in the review protocol or other clinically relevant outcomes. Consequently, additional data could not be obtained. Nine trials provided usable data for the review. Most of the included studies were small in scale and exhibited a high risk of bias. No nutritional interventions were identified as definitively beneficial. For interventions of uncertain effectiveness, postoperative enteral nutrition appeared to have no significant advantage or disadvantage compared to postoperative parenteral nutrition in terms of clinical outcomes. Parenteral nutrition containing protein, fat, carbohydrates, and branched-chain amino acids, with or without alanyl-glutamine, did not improve one-year or three-year survival rates compared to a solution of 5% dextrose and normal saline. Similarly, enteral immunonutrition with Supportan® showed no effect on the incidence of immunological rejection when compared to enteral nutrition with Fresubin®. There is weak evidence suggesting that adding a nutritional supplement to the usual diet during the waiting period for liver transplantation may influence clinical outcomes after the procedure. The combination of enteral nutrition, parenteral nutrition, and glutamine-dipeptide supplementation was associated with a reduced hospital stay duration compared to standard parenteral nutrition (MD -12.20 days; 95% CI -20.20 to -4.00). Weak evidence also indicated that parenteral nutrition with branched-chain amino acids reduced the length of stay in the intensive care unit (ICU) compared to a standard glucose solution (MD -2.40 days; 95% CI -4.29 to -0.51 and MD -2.20 days; 95% CI -3.79 to -0.61, respectively). Additionally, the inclusion of omega-3 fish oil in parenteral nutrition was associated with a shorter hospital stay (MD -7.1 days; 95% CI -13.02 to -1.18) and ICU stay (MD -1.9 days; 95% CI -1.9 to -0.22) after liver transplantation. For interventions deemed unlikely to be beneficial, malnourished patients with a history of encephalopathy who were treated with the nutritional supplement Ensure® had a significantly increased risk of acute rejection compared to those who received only standard dietary advice (MD 0.70 events per patient; 95% CI 0.08 to 1.32). In conclusion, this review did not identify any nutritional interventions for liver-transplanted patients that provided clear and convincing benefits. Further randomized clinical trials with robust sample sizes and low risk of bias are necessary to establish the efficacy of these interventions.
